newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK activists vow to defy China's protest ban.
newsitem.headline: HK activists vow to defy China's protest ban.

text.p: Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists on Thursday vowed to defy a Beijing warning that rallies marking the 1989 crushing of protests at Tiananmen Square would not be tolerated after the handover to China.

More than 150 years of colonial rule end when Hong Kong reverts to China next July 1 under a 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration that pledges the territory considerable autonomy and the right to maintain capitalist freedoms for 50 years.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen told the Asian Wall Street Journal on Wednesday that Hong Kong activists would not be able to mark the bloody June 4, 1989, crackdown on pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.
"In the future, Hong Kong should not hold activities which directly interfere in the affairs of the mainland," Qian was quoted as saying.
He was responding to a question about whether China would permit commemorations to continue beyond the handover.
"It was obvious China would not really treat Hong Kong as an autonomous Special Administrative Region of China," the Hong Kong Economic Journal said.
But Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang argued Qian's remarks had been "wrongly extended" and marked no shift in Chinese policy on post-handover Hong Kong.
Hong Kong radio reported on Thursday evening that London would press Beijing to clarify Qian's remarks.

Radio Television Hong Kong quoted Kerry McGlynn, spokesman for Governor Chris Patten, as saying clarification by the Chinese Foreign Ministry had not provided the reassurance Hong Kong people were seeking and a full explanation was needed.
"(Qian) was unambiguous," the South China Morning Post newspaper said in an editorial that castigated China for threatening the fabric of the 1984 Sino-British treaty.
"This blows a hole not only in the Joint Declaration as generally interpreted, but also threatens the powers and position of the future Hong Kong authorities," the paper said.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement vowed no surrender and said their annual commemorations would continue.

In June this year tens of thousands of Hong Kong people turned out to remember those who died around Tiananmen Square, staging a candle-lit vigil late into the night, a ritual that has evolved into a tradition in the community of six million people.
In 1989 over one million people braved an impending typhoon and took to the streets to express horror at the crackdown, which remains branded in Hong Kong's collective memory.

"Of course, we will continue commemorating those who died in China's democracy movement," Cheung Man-kwong, a leader of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriot Democratic Movements in China, told Reuters.

"Commemoration is not illegal under Hong Kong laws," he said. "China cannot just single out on the law book that the June 4 commemoration is illegal, while allowing patriotic activities to be held in Hong Kong, such as fund-raising galas for victims of flood in southern China."
Alliance member Albert Ho said Qian's comment showed Chinese authorities had no respect for the rule of law.
"Every time they give an interview to foreign media, they put new limits on Hong Kong's laws after 1997," Ho said.
In a rare interview with foreign media in June, Lu Ping, the senior Chinese official in charge of Hong Kong affairs, said press freedom would continue in Hong Kong.
But he warned that Hong Kong media would not be permitted to advocate independence for either Taiwan or Hong Kong itself.
